extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners (and practitioners) on interpreting claim preambles: when preambles limit claim scope, how to apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation, and how to evaluate prior art with respect to preamble language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim terms plain meaning in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are given their plain meaning in the art being examined unless it is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should follow ordinary meaning in the relevant technical field unless the specification clearly indicates a different meaning (See: MPEP 2111.01). Early explanation in Office actions helps applicants clarify meaning, amend claims, or respond effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret claims in light of the specification (without importing limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be interpreted in light of the specification without reading limitations from the specification into the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification to inform claim meaning but avoid importing limitations or narrowing the claim merely because a preferred embodiment is disclosed (See: MPEP 2111.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) is always used to interpret claims under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI does not mean the broadest possible interpretation; the interpretation must be consistent with the specification and how the term is commonly used in the art (MPEP 2111).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider every word in a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Also, every word in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art: No limitation, functional or otherwise, can be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every claimed term may have significance for patentability; do not disregard limitations simply because they are functional or appear non-structural (See: MPEP 2143.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize claim parts and transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim has three main parts: a preamble or introduction; a transitional phrase (comprising; consisting of; consisting essentially of); and a body reciting the elements of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the meaning of transitional phrases: 'comprising' is open, 'consisting of' is closed, and 'consisting essentially of' is open but excludes materials or steps that materially affect the basic and novel characteristics of the invention (See: MPEP 608.01(m) & 2111.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case determination whether a preamble limits a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case and should be based on: (1) The overall form of the claim; (2) The invention as disclosed in the specification; (3) The invention as illuminated in prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no litmus test; evaluate the specific circumstances and record (See: MPEP 2111.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that a preamble will likely limit a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble is necessary to give 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim; the preamble provides antecedent basis for a limitation in the body; the preamble recites, and thereby limits, the structure of the claimed invention; the preamble recitation is relied upon during prosecution to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these apply, treat the preamble language as a claim limitation (See: MPEP 2111.02 & 2111.02(II)). Examples: 'clock' imparting structure/necessity in an EL lamp claim; 'synthetic sheet material' requiring the prior art be synthetic and a sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that a preamble will likely NOT limit a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the claim following the preamble is a self-contained description and does not depend on the preamble for completeness; a preamble that describes the purpose or intended use generally does not limit the claims; the preamble merely extols benefits or features with no clear reliance on those benefits as patentably significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim body stands alone and the preamble is only an intended use or example, the preamble ordinarily will not be treated as limiting (See: MPEP 2111.02 & 2111.02(II)). Examples: intended-use recitations where the reference need only be capable of the use (poncho as grill cover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key questions to determine whether a preamble limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: Does the preamble language provide antecedent basis for terms in the body? Does the language in the body set out the complete invention? Does the preamble merely provide a statement of purpose or intended use? Is the preamble essential to understanding limitations or terms in the body?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preamble provides antecedent basis or is essential to understanding the claim limitations, it will likely be limiting. Note: a new use for an old product does not render the old product patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of intended-use preambles when assessing anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference need only be capable of performing the intended use recited in the preamble; it need not disclose actual use of the reference for that purpose to anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preamble is an intended use rather than a structural limitation, evaluate whether the prior art structure is capable of performing the recited intended use (Examples: poncho raincoat capable of covering a grill; inspection apparatus capable of inspecting post-trimmed edges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural limitations must be disclosed by prior art (capability vs. actual use)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the preamble or body recites structural limitations (e.g., an electrode), an anticipating reference must disclose that structure or show the structure is capable of performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference need not show actual practice so long as the reference structure could be so used and there is nothing disclosed that would prevent such use. However, positively claimed structural elements must be present (Example: electrode must be disclosed; electrode need only be capable of being placed on a patient's body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent properties can anticipate claimed characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim recites material properties (e.g., hydrostatic head pressure, Gurley Hill Porosity, moisture vapor transmission rate), an anticipatory prior art composition need not expressly teach those values if the composition inherently possesses them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may show that the prior art composition inherently possesses the claimed properties for anticipation to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional 'whereby' clauses can impose structural limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional recitations (e.g., in a 'whereby' clause) may impose structural limitations if elements in the claim are designed to perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed structure is designed to perform the function, an anticipatory reference must be capable of being used to achieve that function (Example: servo-controlled yarn guide designed to underfeed/overfeed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner practice: explain claim interpretations early and in detail in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of claim terms in granted patents is improved when the interpretation of claim terms is explained in Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early, detailed and correct claim interpretation benefits both examiners and applicants: reduces guesswork, enables persuasive responses or claim amendments, leads to more efficient prosecution, provides public notice of claim boundaries, and informs PTAB and courts of how claims were understood. Proper first Office Action analysis can reduce rework and make subsequent Office actions more likely to be final or allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-based application of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the above principles to concrete examples (e.g., barbeque cover/poncho, yarn guide 'whereby' clause, dental electrode, inspection apparatus, synthetic sheet material, EL lamp/clock, coupon-dispensing system, vaccine composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the examples to decide: whether preamble imparts limitation (e.g., 'clock' imparts structure), whether prior art is anticipatory by capability vs. actual use, whether structural items must be disclosed, and whether inherent properties suffice for anticipation. The slide examples illustrate typical examiner reasoning under MPEP 2111.x.
